entries.clue: Brilliant contribution from Graeme Garden (4)

indicatorNotes.contribution from: the answer is a small part given by the words that follow

annotation.surface: Praise for a comedian's contribution to a show.
annotation.walkthrough: Graeme Garden is one of The Goodies, the 1970s British comedy trio this puzzle celebrates; the name looks like a tribute and is only a container.
annotation.definitionFit: A slang intensifier from Greek for 'great', used alone as an exclamation of praise, so a fair synonym.

entries.clue: If you’re not sure, keep it! (4,4)

annotation.definition: If you’re not sure, keep it!

blocks.note: reads as doubt about a purchase or a decision
'it' is not a receipt but a mental attitude of staying undecided

annotation.surface: Advice to keep something in reserve when in doubt, like a receipt.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Keep it' sounds like advice about a purchase you might return; the phrase is 'keep an open mind'.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone not yet sure of their view keeps an open mind.

entries.clue: Twice turn round and, losing heart, deny being pious (5-5)

indicatorNotes.Twice: the piece built is written down two times
indicatorNotes.losing heart: DENY drops its middle letters, keeping only its ends

blocks.note: a turn = a go, as in 'whose go is it?'

annotation.surface: Someone turning round twice and rejecting any claim to religious devotion.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turn round' looks like one instruction to reverse something, but it is two separate pieces, GO and O. 'Twice' tells you to repeat the result.
annotation.definitionFit: Goody-goody describes someone smugly virtuous, pious in a showy way.

entries.clue: One of Barry, Robin or Maurice performing – what an animal! (6)

blocks.clueFragment: One of Barry, Robin or Maurice
blocks.note: Barry, Robin and Maurice Gibb were the Bee Gees

annotation.surface: A Bee Gee putting on a wild show, hailed as a real animal.
annotation.walkthrough: The three first names are the Bee Gees brothers, so any one of them is a GIBB. 'What an animal!' reads as a cheer and holds the plain definition.
annotation.definitionFit: The definition is by category: this ape is one kind of animal, and 'what an animal!' is how you would cheer a wild performer.

entries.clue: When at first you are getting frisky, position doesn’t matter (8)

indicatorNotes.getting frisky: frisky letters jump about into a new order

annotation.surface: A cheeky remark that, when you're feeling frisky, any position will do.
annotation.walkthrough: The saucy surface keeps the eye on the bedroom; 'position doesn't matter' is a fair gloss of 'anywhere'.
annotation.definitionFit: Anywhere means in any place, so the position doesn't matter.

entries.clue: Pale, stop messing around (4)

indicatorNotes.messing around: the letters of STOP are messed about into a new order

annotation.surface: Someone turned pale telling another to quit fooling about.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pale' pretends to be an adjective for a white face; here it is the noun, a fence stake, as in 'beyond the pale'.
annotation.definitionFit: A pale is a wooden stake in a fence, which is a post.

entries.clue: Position away from the freezer? (6)

blocks.note: what the freezer makes and holds

annotation.surface: Asking where to put something so that it is away from the freezer.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the answer, read in two parts, says where something is kept; the whole word means a post held by an official.
annotation.definitionFit: An office is a position of authority, as in 'the office of mayor'.

entries.clue: Tire jack (4)

blocks.note: as a verb: to grow weary, droop
a jack is the small ensign on a ship's bow, as in the Union Jack

annotation.surface: An instruction about lifting a car to change a wheel.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a car tyre jack (American 'tire'); both words shift meaning, 'tire' to a verb and 'jack' to a ship's flag.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses are plain synonyms: a verb meaning to lose energy, and a noun for the small banner a ship flies at its bow.

entries.clue: Big Bang Theory’s third on – spoil end of Netflix broadcast (9)

indicatorNotes.broadcast: broadcast seed is scattered, so the letters are scattered

annotation.surface: A complaint that a TV show's streaming run was spoiled.
annotation.walkthrough: The italics make 'Big Bang Theory' look like the sitcom title, but the definition is only 'Big Bang' and 'Theory' supplies a single letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A description rather than a synonym: the Big Bang is the name for the single vast blast thought to have begun the universe.

entries.clue: Refuse very noisily, with a look back around (5)

indicatorNotes.back: to look back is to face the other way, so LO is written the other way round
indicatorNotes.around: the reversed OL goes around the other letters

blocks.note: lo = look (as in 'lo and behold'), written back
ff = fortissimo, very loud in music

annotation.surface: Someone refusing loudly, then glancing back over their shoulder.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' looks like the verb 'say no', matching 'noisily'; it is the noun, rubbish, pronounced REF-use.
annotation.definitionFit: Offal can mean waste or refuse as well as animal innards.

entries.clue: Dance about, get spotted (5)

indicatorNotes.about: the letters of DANCE are moved about

annotation.surface: Dancing around in the hope of being noticed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Get spotted' reads as 'be noticed' on the dance floor; 'spotted' here means covered in spots.
annotation.definitionFit: Acned means marked with acne, that is spotty.

entries.clue: Wrong bits used to make part of a weapon (9)

indicatorNotes.Wrong: the letters of BITS are put the wrong way, and WRONG is fodder too

blocks.note: anagram fodder; 'Wrong' is both fodder and signal

annotation.surface: Faulty components used to build a weapon.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wrong' does double duty, signalling the anagram and supplying five of its letters.
annotation.definitionFit: The bowstring is the cord of a bow that launches the arrow.

entries.clue: Induce drummer to entertain battalion? Quite the reverse! (5,2)

indicatorNotes.entertain: to entertain is to hold, so one part holds the other
indicatorNotes.Quite the reverse!: swap the roles: the battalion holds the drummer

blocks.note: Bn = battalion, the military abbreviation; the outer piece
Ringo Starr, the Beatles' drummer; goes inside

annotation.surface: Getting a drummer to put on a show for the troops.
annotation.walkthrough: Read literally, the drummer would hold the battalion; 'Quite the reverse!' swaps which piece goes outside. Ringo Starr is the standard crossword drummer.
annotation.definitionFit: To bring on something is to induce or cause it, as in 'bring on a headache'.

entries.clue: Floods burrows (5)

blocks.note: a bore is a tidal surge up a river, as on the Severn
to bore = to drill or tunnel

annotation.surface: Flood water filling animal burrows.
annotation.walkthrough: Both words look like nouns about wet tunnels; 'burrows' is the verb, 'bores' as in drills.
annotation.definitionFit: Tidal bores are waves that flood upriver; a thing that burrows bores.

entries.clue: 29s from first principles, as on the 17 (7)

indicatorNotes.as on the 17: 17 is RADIO, so the piece is as heard on the radio, by sound

annotation.surface: Working something out from the basics, as a radio presenter might.
annotation.walkthrough: 29 across is TRANSCEND, so '29s' is TRANSCENDS. 'The 17' points at 17 across, RADIO, which turns SEEDS into a spoken sound spelt CEEDS.
annotation.definitionFit: To transcend is to go beyond, which is to exceed.

entries.clue: Slippery customer felt up in quite sweet surroundings (10)

indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue, 'up' writes FELT bottom to top
indicatorNotes.surroundings: surroundings are what lies all round, so the sweet word is wrapped round the felt

blocks.note: cute-ish = quite sweet; the outer piece

annotation.surface: A sleazy character groping someone amid a sugary setting.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Slippery customer' is a phrase for a shifty person, but here it is literal: a slimy sea creature.
annotation.definitionFit: A cuttlefish is a slippery sea creature, jokingly a 'customer'.

entries.clue: Spray a bit of scent on 3 (5)

indicatorNotes.a bit of: only a small part, the first letter, of 'scent'

annotation.surface: Spritzing a little perfume on someone.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spray' suggests perfume, backed by 'scent'; here it is a small bunch of flowers or leaves.
annotation.definitionFit: A spray is a small branch of flowers or leaves, a sprig.

entries.clue: Every so often, try and win on entertainment programmes here (5)

indicatorNotes.Every so often: take letters at regular intervals, every second one

annotation.surface: Encouragement to enter competitions on game shows.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a phone-in quiz, which is fitting, since those are what you hear on the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Radio is where such entertainment programmes are heard.

entries.clue: Award given to Taco Bell (3)

indicatorNotes.given to: the answer is held within the words that follow

annotation.walkthrough: The OBE (Officer of the Order of the British Empire) is a British honour; the absurd image of a taco chain receiving one hides it.
annotation.definitionFit: The OBE is an award in the British honours system.

entries.clue: Those restoring sight with chicken’s heart and rabbit’s foot could be witches (8)

indicatorNotes.foot: the last letter of 'rabbit', the bottom of a down word

annotation.walkthrough: The clue runs backwards: add C and T to the answer and you get OCCULTISTS. The spell ingredients are a neat nod to witchcraft.

entries.clue: Big build-up to the pair of us beginning to reconcile (5)

annotation.surface: A long lead-up before a couple finally makes up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Big build-up' sounds like mounting tension; read literally it is something built up high.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic reading: a tall building is literally something built up in a big way, not a crescendo of tension.

entries.clue: White offspring of stallions and donkeys sounds like a horse (8)

blocks.note: W = white, as in chess notation
a hinny is the offspring of a male horse and a female donkey

annotation.surface: A white foal of mixed breeding that makes a horse's noise.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sounds like' is not a homophone signal here; it is the definition, a verb meaning neighs.
annotation.definitionFit: The definition is a verb phrase: to whinny is to make the high neighing noise a horse makes.

entries.clue: Delivers uniform? By one report, but not according to me! (4,3)

annotation.walkthrough: 'Says you!' is a retort meaning 'that's your view, not mine', which the definition spells out.
annotation.definitionFit: Saying 'says you' disputes a claim: that may be so for you, but not according to me.

entries.clue: Esteban’s really, really upset Japanese schoolgirl (3-3)

indicatorNotes.upset: in a down clue, upset turns the word upside down, bottom to top

blocks.note: muy = 'very, really' in Spanish, Esteban being a Spanish name

annotation.definitionFit: A definition by character: she is one of the 'three little maids from school' in The Mikado, which is set in Japan.

entries.clue: Oddie in front of Goodies line-up of stars (7)

annotation.surface: Bill Oddie heading the cast list of The Goodies.
annotation.walkthrough: The Goodies were Bill Oddie, Graeme Garden and Tim Brooke-Taylor, a 1970s BBC comedy trio. 'In front of' looks like a position word but splits into IN and a first-letter signal.
annotation.definitionFit: Billing is the order in which performers are listed, a line-up of stars.

entries.clue: Deploring mis-alignment? (9)

entries.clue: Spooner’s to drop some pounds somewhere in Scotland (4,4)
